title: Still Here Without Us
logline: A flat coral island off the country's northern tip where three empires in turn bred horses to sell, and where several hundred of their descendants now cross a bleached plain inside dry-stone walls nobody built for them, no longer worth anything to anybody, and looked at.
human_question: If the useful reason a thing was made for has gone, and the thing is still here, what is left of the wanting that made it — and what is my looking at it?

place.what_kind_of_place: A low island of pale porous coral about ten kilometres off the end of a peninsula, roughly fifty square kilometres, oval, semi-arid, with no relief and no shelter. Palmyra palms, thorn scrub and open dry pasture; two shallow inland lakes that empty in the dry months; a coastline of dead coral outcrop and rubble beach. The whole of it is divided by dry-stone walls built out of blocks of dead reef, laid without mortar, in some places about four metres high, running for kilometres and crossing ground nobody is farming. Standing in the pasture are the roofless remains of a stone stable a hundred and fifty metres long, a set of deep wells with ramps cut down to the water so that animals could walk in, a small square dovecote of limestone, a two-storey coral-and-limestone fort on the shore, a stepped stone tower, ruined stupas, and one enormous hollow baobab, a tree from Africa that does not belong in this ocean. Between four and five thousand people live on the island, most of it inhabited at the northern end; the southern plains, where the horses are, were gazetted as a national park. There is one crossing, a boat of about an hour.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things carry it with the sound off, and none of them needs a word. First, the geometry from the air: a pale flat island in a very shallow, very bright sea, ruled across its whole width by a grid of white walls that is plainly the work of somebody and plainly serves nothing now, with the sea visible on two or three sides of almost every frame. Second, the stable at ground level — two rows of thirty-six square pillars, a hundred and fifty metres of open colonnade with the sky where the roof was, photographed in flat white noon light, which is the single most beautiful frame the island produces and is also, exactly, the argument. Third, the animals: small hardy pale-brown horses at the far end of a long lens, doing nothing, at their own distance, in a landscape that has nothing else vertical in it. The film is the group's emptiest and its widest, and it is deliberately airless: hard light, salt, wind, no crowd, no interior, no golden hour, no drone push.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The wind, the light and the water, and the animals when they choose to. Nothing is arranged and nothing is made to happen: if the herd is standing still for forty minutes, the film has forty minutes of a herd standing still. The walls change entirely with the sun's angle — at noon they are a flat white line, and within an hour they are throwing a hard black edge across the pasture. The pasture itself changes across the year, from thin green after the north-east rains to bleached grey-yellow by the end of the dry months, when the inland water is gone and the wildlife department brings water in by bowser to troughs. The sea goes from grey to a hard pale green. Nothing about the place builds towards anything, which is why the film has to be built out of the walls, the stable and the distance rather than out of an event.
place.when_it_looks_best: The late dry season, roughly June to September, when the pasture is bleached, the walls are at their whitest, the light is flat and hard for most of the day and the horses are concentrated near water. That is also when the animals are under most pressure, which is a reason for more distance and less time, not less. The rains come around October to February and green the pasture; the crossing is least reliable in rough weather. Middle of the day is the film's own hour, which is unusual for this slate and is the point: nothing here is flattered.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A wide, dry, wind-scoured island film with no people in it and no story being told. A boat crosses shallow water; a pale island appears, ruled across with white walls; a colonnade of stone pillars stands roofless in a field; a well goes down into the ground with a ramp for animals; a hollow tree stands alone; horses move very far away and then do not move; the sea is on every side. It resolves on its own terms — arrival, the built things, the animals, the empty pasture — and someone who never hears a word of the narration gets a complete, austere, strangely beautiful piece about a place that was clearly made for something and is not doing it any more.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the group's cleanest handling of its own hazard, because there is no face in it at all. The voice does not accuse anyone. It sets out what the old Sinhala compendium actually says: that earning, guarding and spending are on its list of ordinary occasions for wanting, that this is a description of most of a working day and not a charge, and that the very same acts are expressly not counted against anyone when they are done out of faith, kindness, compassion, or with a practical eye to what is useful. Then it says where the compendium does draw its line, which is at beauty — at catching a fine animal because you saw it, and at keeping one so that it can be looked at. Three empires bred these animals to sell, which engages the exemption. Nobody breeds them now; they have no commercial value; the one purpose left on the island is that people come and look at them, and the camera is one of those people. The film ends by turning the doctrine onto itself instead of onto the past or onto anyone living.

sequence.on_screen: The crossing, then the island from very high: a flat pale shape in bright shallow water, ruled edge to edge by a grid of white walls, with no field being worked inside any of them.
sequence.voice: Somebody built all of this. The old Sinhala compendium of mind has a list of the ordinary occasions on which wanting arises, and it is a long and undramatic list: earning wealth, getting it, guarding what has been got, spending it to obtain the things one likes, and putting those things together and using them.

sequence.on_screen: Ground level, flat white noon. A roofless colonnade in open pasture: two rows of thirty-six square pillars, a hundred and fifty metres end to end, a gable wall still standing at one end. Dry grass through the floor.
sequence.voice: This was a stable. An Irish lieutenant in a British colonial regiment built three like it, and he was given the horses to breed the year after he was given a flax crop to grow for canvas. Portuguese writers had already called this the island of cows and then the island of horses; the Dutch renamed it after a town at home and bred and sold from it; the British wanted cavalry mounts. The compendium is not accusing any of them. It says only that for people living at a distance from the teaching, most of the minds between waking and sleeping are of this kind. It is a description of an ordinary working day.

sequence.on_screen: A well: a stone shaft with a ramp cut down into it so an animal can walk to the water. Then a metal trough in the pasture, and a water tank standing on bare ground. No person in frame.
sequence.voice: He also cut wells, with ramps, for his stock. They are still the island's best fresh water. And here the compendium makes the distinction the whole film rests on. Earning, guarding and spending are not counted against a person when they are done out of faith, out of loving-kindness, out of compassion, or with practical discernment of what is actually useful. A stud farm that supplied mounts and transport is squarely inside that. Feeding an animal as a kindness the book calls outright good.

sequence.on_screen: The walls at eye level: blocks of dead reef stacked without mortar, four metres in places, running away to the horizon across ground nobody is cultivating. Then a gap in one, wide open, with nothing on either side of it.
sequence.voice: There is a separate item in these books for the wish to take a thing up, and both of them go out of their way to say it is not greed. Greed is the sticking. This is only the reaching, and it takes the colour of whatever it joins. Three hundred years of reaching is standing here in dead coral, four metres high, holding nothing in and nothing out.

sequence.on_screen: Long lens, from as far back as the frame allows. Small pale-brown horses at the other end of the pasture, standing, grazing, walking off at their own speed. The camera does not follow them and never closes the distance.
sequence.voice: The books say effort is the part that does not turn back until what was started is finished, and they are careful that this is not a virtue. Their picture for it is a boat: on a current running the way the mind already leans it goes easily, and the other way is a load carried uphill. The reaching did not turn back here for three centuries. Then it stopped, and nothing about these animals changed except that nobody wanted anything from them.

sequence.on_screen: The hollow baobab, an African tree standing alone on coral, a doorway-sized opening into its trunk. Then the small limestone dovecote with its rows of holes, empty.
sequence.voice: Two more things brought here to be used: a tree that stores water in its own trunk, and a house for pigeons that carried letters to the mainland. And now the line the compendium draws. Catching a fine animal because you saw it, and keeping one in order to look at how fine it is, are named on the wanting side — not the practical side. Nobody breeds or sells these animals. The wildlife report says plainly that they have no commercial value, and that the viewing of them could be developed for visitors. The only purpose left on this island is looking at them, and a camera is what looking looks like.

sequence.on_screen: The herd walks out of frame at its own pace. The camera holds the empty bleached pasture, the walls, the wind in the grass, and the sea beyond on two sides. Hold long. Cut.
sequence.voice: They are not free and they are not a lesson. They are several hundred small horses on a dry coral island in a bad year, and nobody agrees on how many. The books will not let the word be used as an accusation even so, because they say that the same reaching, trained and pointed, is what carries a person the whole way. The reaching was never the problem. Whatever will not let go was, and it let go of this place a long time ago.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, C005 is a list of occasions and a rule for sorting them, and C021 is an anatomy of the working parts. C005's list of occasions is explicitly economic: doing various things to earn wealth, obtaining it, guarding what has been obtained, spending it to get desirable objects, and preparing and consuming those objects [C005-M:L5], and the Margaya adds that for people living apart from the teaching most of the minds between waking and sleep are of this kind [C005-M:L7] — a description of a working day, not a charge sheet. Then it draws its line by aim and not by act: the same earning, guarding, spending and provisioning is expressly not unwholesome when done with faith, loving-kindness or compassion foremost, or with practical discernment of usefulness [C005-M:L9], and feeding animals as a kindness it calls outright wholesome, as against feeding them for the pleasure of watching [C005-M:L21]. And it puts beauty on the other side, twice and specifically: catching a fine animal on seeing it, and keeping one in order to look at its beauty, are greed-rooted [C005-M:L23]. That pairing of L9 against L23 is the whole film, because the island's history is an enterprise with a practical purpose and its present is an animal kept by nobody and looked at. C021 supplies what stops the film from becoming a verdict. Desire-to-act is the wish to take a thing up and is not the force that makes one stick to it; the sticking force has its own names [C021-P:L69], and the Margaya says it looks a little like greed but has no adhering quality at all and takes the moral side of whatever mind it joins [C021-M:L27]. Effort is the part that does not turn back until the task is finished [C021-M:L19] and it has no colour of its own, running easily downhill in a mind already leaning and uphill in one that is not [C021-P:L53]. Three empires' worth of reaching is standing on this island in dead coral, and nothing is being held.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That an appetite can leave its whole apparatus behind and be gone from it, and that the apparatus is not the appetite. C005 alone would make this a film about colonial greed, which the source itself refuses, since it sorts by aim and no ledger records an aim. C021 alone would make it a film about drive and craft with nothing at stake. Together they produce a single frame that does both jobs at once: a roofless stone colonnade a hundred and fifty metres long, in flat white light, with dry grass growing through the floor of it. It is the most beautiful thing on the island and it is the concept exactly — the reaching, built at enormous cost, in full view, with nothing stuck to it. The pairing also forces the film's one honest move. C005's line at beauty [C005-M:L23] does not fall on the breeders, whose purpose was practical and therefore exempt under its own rule [C005-M:L9]; it falls on the only remaining relation anyone has to these animals, which is that people come and look at them. The film therefore ends by turning the doctrine onto its own camera rather than onto the empire or onto anyone living on the island, which is both the truthful reading and the only one the floor permits.

concept_links.why: The Margaya's occasions are the exact economic acts this island was organised for: doing various things to earn wealth, obtaining it, guarding what has been obtained, and spending it to get the objects one likes [C005-M:L5], with the note that most of an ordinary person's day runs this way [C005-M:L7]. Its rule is what makes the film possible without an accusation, because it sorts by aim and not by act: the same earning, guarding, spending and provisioning is not counted as unwholesome when done with faith, loving-kindness or compassion foremost, or with practical discernment of usefulness [C005-M:L9]. A breeding station supplying mounts, haulage and cavalry engages that exemption on its face, and the digest's own uncertainty is load-bearing here — the source never says what kind of mind the exempted cases are instead, so the film leaves that gap open rather than filling it with praise. The line the source does draw lands on beauty, and it lands on this subject unusually precisely: catching a fine animal because you saw it, and keeping one so that its beauty can be looked at, are named as greed-rooted [C005-M:L23], and the neighbouring ruling separates feeding an animal for the pleasure of watching from feeding it as a kindness, which it calls wholesome outright [C005-M:L21]. That is why the beat about the water troughs is the one unambiguously good thing the film names, and why the beat about visitors and cameras is the one place the doctrine is applied to anybody. Three of the digest's limits do real work. It is not a case for austerity, since the source allows wealth earned and spent wisely, so the enterprise is never made to look shabby. It does not dissolve everything into motive, since it still names seven particular courses of action as harm done through wanting — theft, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, idle chatter, covetousness and view [C005-M:L3] — and the taking of life is not among them, which is why no beat is built on animal death and the dry-season mortality is stated once, flat, as drought. And it must not be used to frame any living person: the ruling at [C005-M:L23] describes a mind, no camera can photograph one, and in this group in particular no identifiable person may carry the wanting. The voice therefore applies that line to the film's own presence and to nobody else's.

C021 keeps the film from mistaking the apparatus for the appetite. Desire-to-act is the wish to take the object up and is explicitly not the force that makes one adhere to it; the adhering force is named separately as greed and craving [C021-P:L69], and the Margaya says it resembles greed a little but has no adhering quality, being a wanting without stickiness that accords with greed in a greed-accompanied mind and opposes it in a mind set against greed [C021-M:L27]. Standing in front of four metres of mortarless dead coral running to the horizon, that distinction is not an abstraction: the reaching is physically present and nothing is stuck to it. Effort supplies the duration. It is the part that does not retreat and goes forward until what was begun is finished, and it is mental rather than bodily [C021-M:L19]; the source's boat image makes it morally neutral, easy as a boat on a downstream current where a mind already leans, and a load carried uphill where it does not [C021-P:L53]. Three centuries of stock-breeding on a waterless island is that neutrality at full scale. Two further pieces are available and one of them is used with care. The six factors are called scattered because, unlike the universal ones, they are present in some minds and absent in others across both the wholesome and the unwholesome sides [C021-P:L25] [C021-M:L3] — which is the source's own reason why no state can be read off a landscape or an animal. And decision settles firmly on an object without distinguishing true from false or good from bad, so that it is frequently firm and wrong [C021-P:L45], while the Margaya calls it hard to discern at all [C021-M:L15]: the film uses that only as a guard, never to imply that the crew knows which of the island's competing figures and attributions is the correct one. The digest's cautions are the film's rails. Not follow-your-passion, because desire-to-act inside a greed-rooted mind strengthens the greed. Not hard-work-as-virtue, because effort is neutral. Not desire-is-the-enemy, because the source says the opposite — developed, desire-to-act becomes a base of success that subdues craving and leads the whole way [C021-P:L75], which is what the last beat exists to say. And the source's account of gladness moving the body through the air element is traditional physiology, which the digest rules out as a modern claim, so no animal's movement is ever narrated as delight.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That an appetite is not the same thing as the works it leaves standing, and that the old analysis sorts an act by what it was for rather than by what it was. The proof needs no vocabulary: a hundred and fifty metres of roofless stone colonnade with grass through the floor, kilometres of dry-stone wall holding nothing in, deep wells with ramps for animals that no longer need to be led anywhere — and, at the far end of a long lens, the animals themselves, worth nothing to anybody, which is the only reason people come. A viewer should leave able to say what the difference is between reaching for something and being unable to let it go, and should not leave with the impression that anyone in the film's history has been judged, or that the horses stand for freedom.
what_must_be_real: The animals' distance is not negotiable and is the film's first condition. They are filmed on a long lens from as far away as the frame allows. They are never driven, baited, fed, called, cornered, herded, chased, blocked, followed on foot or by vehicle, flown at, or made to move for any frame; if the herd moves away, that is the end of the shot. No drone goes near them at any altitude that alters their behaviour, and if drone flight is permitted at all it stays over the walls, the ruins and the pasture, not over animals. No sound is played or made to get an ear or a head turn. Nothing is staged with a captive or ridden animal, and the island's practice of lassoing wild horses from horseback is not filmed, arranged, requested or reconstructed under any circumstances, whatever is offered. Dry-season mortality is real and documented; a dead animal is not photographed, and the deaths are stated once in the voice as drought and never as consequence or as a warning. The island's residents are not scenery: nobody is filmed as texture in a landscape film, no house, yard, boat or burial ground is used for atmosphere, no islander is framed as a keeper, a poacher or a picturesque inhabitant, consent is asked in Tamil by someone who speaks it, and if the film cannot be made without using people as local colour it is not made. The walls, the stable, the wells, the dovecote, the tower and the fort are filmed as they stand, unswept, unlit and uncleared, with no chalking, wetting or dressing of stone, and the gazetted archaeological monument and the national park are entered only under written permission. The competing accounts of who brought the horses and how many there are go in the voice as competing accounts or not at all; no figure is presented as a count.
position_hint: late in the group, and probably last: it is the only film here with no human subject at all, and it works best after the films in which the wanting still has somebody doing it, so that an island where the wanting has simply stopped reads as the group's conclusion rather than as an absence. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Making the horses a symbol of freedom, resilience or wildness reclaiming a colony. This is the single likeliest failure, it is what every existing photograph of this place does, and the last beat exists to refuse it in words while the long lens refuses it in framing.

Narrating the empire's appetite as irony — the walls that hold nothing, the stable with no roof, the wells for horses that now water people. The material is all there and the tone is forbidden; every one of those facts is stated flat, once, as a fact.

Letting any identifiable person carry the wanting, which is this group's specific hazard. Nobody on the island is shown as acquisitive, and the one place the source's ruling on beauty is applied to a living relation [C005-M:L23] is applied to the film's own camera.

Turning the source's exemption into praise of the colonists. The rule sorts by aim [C005-M:L9] and the digest notes that the source does not say what the exempted cases are instead; the archive records acts, toponyms, gazettes and ledgers, and never an aim, so the film states the exemption and stops.
An austerity reading, in which the ruined enterprise becomes a lesson against wealth. The digest rules it out: the source allows wealth earned and spent wisely and does not preach deprivation.

Building an argument on animal suffering or animal death. The seven courses of action the source attributes to wanting do not include the taking of life [C005-M:L3], and the film's subject is the walls and the purpose, not the mortality.
Reading effort as virtue, or three centuries of breeding as admirable persistence. The source's own image makes effort morally neutral and dependent only on the slope it is put on [C021-P:L53].
Reading the film as desire-is-the-enemy. The source says the opposite of desire-to-act, which developed subdues craving and leads to the highest good [C021-P:L75].

Presenting any population figure as a count. The wildlife department's own park publication gives about four hundred to five hundred in one section and about a thousand in another, and no census was found; a confident number on screen would be exactly the firm-and-wrong settling the source describes [C021-P:L45].
Treating the island's people as local colour in a film that has deliberately removed all human subjects. A landscape film about somebody's home is the version of this idea that breaks the floor.

Animal welfare in the act of filming: a herd under water stress in the late dry season is the worst possible subject to approach, and the film's own best season is the season in which it must keep furthest away.

Access and permissions stacked three deep — a national park under the wildlife department, a gazetted archaeological monument, and drone rules over a northern island with naval facilities and a naval-operated ferry. The film's widest shots may simply not be allowed.
Filming inside the hollow baobab, or making the tree a mystical object. It is a tree from Africa on coral, and that is the whole of what the film says about it.
drop_if: The horses cannot be filmed at a distance that leaves them entirely undisturbed, or the only offered access to them involves driving, baiting, penning or lassoing.
Permission for the pasture inside the national park is refused and there is no lawful position from which the animals can be filmed without approaching them.
The stable, the walls and the wells cannot be filmed, in which case the film has lost its argument and keeps only its animals, which is the version that must not be made.
The film can only be made by using the island's residents as scenery, or consent cannot properly be asked in Tamil.
Conditions of access require a flattering account of the site's development as a tourist attraction, or require the competing origin stories and population figures to be presented as settled.

connections.note: Direct location overlap, recorded here so it is not lost: IDEA-0044 is set on the same island, at its administrative office, and is due to be replaced in GRP-03's own pass. The two films share nothing but the ground. That one is an interior about a numbered queue bracketed by a ferry timetable, built on restlessness and displeasure, shot in a room at mid-morning with a grille shadow crossing a tiled floor, with staff and members of the public in frame under written permission. This one has no interior, no queue, no institution in operation and no person in frame at all; it is exterior, long-lens, flat noon light, and its subject is an enterprise that closed two centuries ago. If both records somehow survive, this one keeps the walls, the stable, the wells, the dovecote, the baobab and the horses, and does not use the ferry as a constraint, the office, or any counter.

The slate's other film about coral as building material. That one is a southern coast where the living reef was cut, carried up the beach and burned into lime that now stands in the plaster of houses, and it ends underwater on reef restoration. This one has no lime, no kiln, no underwater work and no argument about a lost reef; its coral is dead blocks stacked dry into field walls on a northern island, and the walls are evidence of a purpose, not of an extraction.

The slate's other film about a protected place left to itself. That one is a small offshore reserve being deliberately shut for a season by the people who run it, and its subject is the closing. Here nothing is being closed and nobody is leaving: the institution left in the nineteenth century, the protection arrived in the twenty-first, and the film is about the gap.

The group's other national park, reassigned in the same pass to a cold high plateau. That film is cloud, wet tussock and grey; this one is hard white light, salt and no relief at all. Between them the group's two protected-area films share no weather, no altitude, no colour and no lens length.

selection.reason: The group's only animal film and its only island, and the one place on the slate where the compendium's sorting rule can be shown rather than argued: a working enterprise whose practical purpose engages the source's own exemption, and a present in which the only remaining purpose is the one the source names on the other side. It is also the group's only film with no human subject in it, which is the cleanest possible answer to the group's hazard.

review.note: Written fresh on 2026-09-26 and the verdict reset with it; the previous body is gone and any earlier judgement refers to nothing. The old film was a pre-dawn fish auction on a northern beach, built on rings of buyers closing around each catch and opening when the price was found. It went for the reason the whole group is being reworked: it was a working place carrying the philosophy by analogy, with no documented or disputed story in it, and its central overhead shot depended on drone permission next to a harbour under military oversight. It also put a crowd of identifiable working people in front of a camera in a group about greed, which is the hazard this group exists to avoid. The historical binding is now the argument rather than the setting. Three colonial powers in turn ran stock-breeding on one low coral island: Portuguese writers of the 1597-1658 occupation called it the island of cows and then the island of horses; the Dutch, who took the north in 1658, renamed it after a town at home, bred there and distributed animals by sea; and under the British, Lieutenant Edward Nolan of the 4th Ceylon Regiment was set to grow flax for canvas in 1811 and given the horses to breed the following year, built three stone stables and a set of ramped wells that are still the island's best fresh water, shipped surplus animals to a neighbouring islet for pasturage, and left in 1824. That history is the concept, because C005 sorts an act by its aim rather than by the act itself: earning, guarding and spending are on its list of occasions for wanting [C005-M:L5], and the same acts are expressly not counted against anyone when done from faith, loving-kindness, compassion or a practical sense of usefulness [C005-M:L9], which a stud farm supplying mounts and haulage engages on its face. What the source does put on the wanting side, twice and specifically, is beauty: catching a fine animal because you saw it, and keeping one in order to look at its beauty [C005-M:L23]. Nobody breeds or sells these animals now, the 2013 IUCN assessment records that they have no commercial value and proposes viewing them as a tourist product, and the film therefore turns that one ruling onto its own camera rather than onto the empire or onto anyone living on the island. C021 supplies the guard: the wish to take a thing up is not greed, greed is the sticking [C021-P:L69] [C021-M:L27], and effort has no colour of its own [C021-P:L53], so kilometres of dry-stone wall and a roofless colonnade are the reaching with nothing stuck to it. The guards, in full: the animals are filmed at long-lens distance and are never driven, baited, cornered, chased or made to move for a frame, and the island's surviving practice of lassoing wild horses from horseback is not filmed or arranged in any form; they are not presented as symbols of freedom, which is the failure every existing picture of this place makes and which the last beat refuses in words; the empire's appetite is never narrated as irony, although the material invites it at every turn; the island's four to five thousand residents are not local colour and no person appears in frame at all; no identifiable person carries the wanting, which is this group's specific hazard; the dry-season deaths are stated once as drought and never as consequence, because kamma is not fate and because the taking of life is not among the seven courses of action the source attributes to wanting [C005-M:L3]; and the colonial layers are recorded and never adjudicated. Research corrected the brief at three points and they are recorded in the thread rather than smoothed: the coral walls are not Dutch and were probably not built to pen horses, the figure of five hundred horses has no traceable basis and the wildlife department's own publication prints two irreconcilable numbers, and the stables and wells popularly attributed to the Dutch were built by a British officer, as the IUCN assessment states explicitly. Title kept from the reassignment row; both previous titles are in aliases.

suggested_location.region: Jaffna District, Northern Province: the outermost inhabited island west of the peninsula, about 10 km offshore in the Palk Strait, reached by boat from the Kurikadduwan jetty on Punkudutivu. The southern part of the island is Delft National Park
suggested_location.why_here: It is the only place that hands the film the concept and the frame in the same shot. C005 sorts an act by its aim and not by the act, and this island is a whole landscape built for one aim that has gone: three colonial administrations in turn bred horses here to sell, and what stands in the pasture now is a hundred and fifty metres of roofless stone colonnade with two rows of thirty-six pillars, kilometres of mortarless dead-coral wall up to about four metres high crossing ground nobody cultivates, and deep wells with ramps cut so animals could walk down to water. Every one of those is the reaching, at scale, in daylight, with nothing held. And the animals are still here, several hundred of them, worth nothing to anybody by the wildlife assessment's own account, which puts the source's ruling about keeping a beautiful animal in order to look at it exactly on the film's own presence rather than on the past. The place also gives the group a treatment it has nowhere else: flat, low, treeless, salt-scoured, hard white noon light, sea on every horizon, no crowd, no interior, no monument, a long lens and a camera that mostly does not move. The group's only island and its only animals.

historical_thread.story:
The island is low, porous coral, about fifty square kilometres, ten kilometres off the end of the Jaffna peninsula in the Palk Strait, and it has been used as grazing ground by every power that held the north.

The Portuguese held Jaffna from 1597 to 1658, and their writing gives the island two successive names that are themselves the record of what it was for: Ilha das Vacas, the island of cows, and then Ilha das Cavallos, the island of horses. The Portuguese are reported to have built a fort on the coast, ploughed the ground to make artificial pasture for horses and cattle, and introduced the horses; the same accounts add that they taught the islanders to use a lasso. No Portuguese document naming the importation was found in this research, and the attribution in the modern literature rests on the toponyms, on a Dutch account written later, and on a twentieth-century survey of the British-period records.

The Dutch took Jaffna from the Portuguese in 1658. Rijckloff van Goens named the eight principal islands of the group after Dutch cities, and this one became Delft. The earliest description of the horses located here is by Philippus Baldaeus, the minister of the Dutch Reformed Church who accompanied the troops that took Jaffna, in his description of Malabar, Coromandel and Ceylon published in 1672; as quoted in the IUCN assessment he writes of 'these horses that were brought into the Delft, which, multiplying in time, produced a certain kind of horses that are very small but hardy and fit to travel on stony and rocky ground ... they live in the wilderness and are taken by catching them in snares or ropes'. Two things follow from that sentence and they are easy to miss. Within about fourteen years of the Dutch arrival the animals were already described as living in the wild and being harvested by snare rather than kept in a stud; and Baldaeus does not say who brought them. The same assessment records that in the Dutch period the island was used to breed and distribute imported horses, and the wildlife department's own park publication says they were bred by the Dutch and sold to ships passing the island. It is also Baldaeus's illustration that is used to argue that the surviving coral-and-limestone fort on the coast is Portuguese rather than Dutch; Katiresu identified it as a Dutch fort in 1905, Nelson rejected that in 1984, and later books list it as Portuguese.

The British period is the best documented and it is where most of what a visitor sees today was actually built. In 1811 Lieutenant Edward Nolan, an Irishman of the 4th Ceylon Regiment serving in the Engineers Division under the Right Honourable John Wilson, Lieutenant-Governor and Commander-in-Chief of the British settlements in Ceylon, was set the task of growing flax on the island to supply the government with canvas. The following year he was additionally given the task of breeding the horses that the Portuguese and Dutch settlers had introduced, and he brought in several new breeding stocks. As the Empire expanded and cavalry demand grew, the island could not grow fodder for the numbers it was carrying and animals were shipped to the small neighbouring island of Iranaitivu for pasturage; the island came to be known as the Horse Plains. Nolan built three sets of stone stables — one for untamed animals, one for trained ones and one for training — and a series of wells ingeniously cut with ramps down to the water so that stock could walk in; those wells remain the island's principal source of fresh water. He built a mansion that can no longer be located, kept about sixty pigeons in a limestone dovecote to carry messages to the peninsula, and was the subject in 1819 of a petition signed by forty-five islanders and sent to the British Resident at Jaffna over his conduct towards the women of the island; the charges were dismissed and he ruled the island until he retired and returned to Ireland in 1824. Two stone towers on the island are British navigational and trigonometric points, of which the one called the Queen's Tower survives to about fifty-five feet in five diminishing stages, while only the base of the King's Tower remains.

The field walls are the thing most often got wrong. Philip K. Crowe, the United States ambassador who toured the island in 1954 and worked through the British records to identify its monuments, attributes the island's characteristic walls to Nolan: they are Irish-style field fences, which in Ireland are built of rock and here are built of coral, and Crowe records that the islanders had continued the practice, as they still do. Crowe also observed of the horses that the stallions appeared better than the mares and that no new blood had been introduced since Nolan's time in 1824. The IUCN assessment states flatly that the stables and wells built by Nolan are at present attributed to the Dutch by the island's inhabitants and by recently published tourist guides, and Sri Lankan heritage sites indeed carry them under the Dutch name. The surviving stable, in Sarappiddy, is about a hundred and fifty metres long and ten metres wide, built on two rows of thirty-six square pillars about three feet thick, with a gable wall about six metres high and many columns broken; it was maintained by successive administrators until 1870 and then abandoned, and it was declared a protected archaeological monument by gazette notification No. 1868 of 20 June 2014.

The present arrangement is recent. The Government of Sri Lanka and IUCN published an ecological, socio-economic and archaeological assessment of the island in January 2013 (Goonatilake, Ekanayake, Kumara, Liyanapathirana, Weerakoon and Wadugodapitiya), which recommended that the southern part of the island be declared a protected area for the horses; an integrated strategic environmental assessment for the northern province repeated the recommendation in October 2014; and 1,846.2 hectares of the island were declared Delft National Park under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance by special gazette notification dated 22 June 2015, managed by the Department of Wildlife Conservation. The 2013 assessment records the horses as a feral population of Equus caballus in the island's grassland habitats, notes that except for a few families who keep captive animals they have no commercial value and are allowed to roam at the far end of the island, and observes that the viewing of them could be developed as a product for tourists. It also records two live problems: cattle released to graze because there is no fodder compete with the horses for pasture, and people capture and mark the ponies' calves with improper branding methods, which causes infections and is a major cause of death among calves. Press reporting adds that the animals generally carry brands, that many of them therefore still have owners although all are left to roam, and that islanders still take them with snares, sidling up to a herd on domesticated horses and surrounding a few. In the 2011 dry season the Divisional Secretary, Alavipillai Siri, reported that about five per cent of the wild horse and cattle populations died for want of water, and the navy built troughs; the wildlife department now brings water in by bowser to tanks in the park, and its own publication says that animals die during that period regardless. The island's other notable introduction is a single large hollow baobab, Adansonia digitata, an African tree held to have been brought to South Asia by Arab sailors and locally said to have been planted in the seventh century or in the sixteenth, depending on the account.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C005 sorts a wanting act by its aim and not by the act, and this island is the rare case where the act is enormous, fully documented and still standing, while the aim is exactly what the archive cannot supply. That gap is the film.

The acts are on the Margaya's own list, almost item for item. Doing various things in order to earn wealth: ploughing a coral island into artificial pasture, importing breeding stock, growing flax for canvas. Guarding what has been obtained: three stables, one for untamed animals, one for trained ones and one for training. Spending in order to get the things one likes: new breed stocks brought in, wells cut with ramps so animals could walk down to water, surplus animals shipped to another island because this one could not feed them [C005-M:L5]. And the Margaya's flat, unshocked note that for people living at a distance from the teaching most of the minds between waking and sleeping are of this kind [C005-M:L7] is the correct register for all of it; nothing here is exceptional, which is why the film can film it without an accusation.

Then the rule. The same earning, guarding, spending and provisioning is expressly not counted as unwholesome when it is done with faith, loving-kindness or compassion foremost, or with practical discernment of what is useful [C005-M:L9]. Mounts, haulage and cavalry remounts are a practical purpose on their face, and the exemption therefore covers the enterprise as a matter of the source's own rule. But the exemption turns on an aim, and the record contains no aim anywhere. It contains two Portuguese place-names, a Dutch minister's sentence about small hardy horses taken with ropes, a lieutenant's two tasks in consecutive years, a shipping arrangement to a neighbouring islet, three stables, a set of wells, a petition, a retirement date, a gazette. Ledgers and gazettes record acts. The line the doctrine draws runs exactly where the archive stops, which is why the film states the exemption and then stops too, and why the digest's own note that the source never says what the exempted cases are instead is left open rather than filled in.

What the source does place on the wanting side, twice, is beauty — and it does so in terms that are almost uncomfortably close to this subject: catching a fine animal because one has seen it, and keeping or feeding one in order to look at how fine it is, are greed-rooted [C005-M:L23]; and the adjacent ruling separates feeding an animal for the pleasure of watching it eat from feeding it as a kindness, which it calls wholesome outright [C005-M:L21]. Held against the present state of the island, those two lines sort the whole of it. The breeding is exempt as practical. The water bowsers and troughs, which keep animals alive in the drought for no return, are the film's one unambiguously wholesome item, and the source says so in as many words. And the one purpose left — the assessment's own recommendation that the viewing of these horses be developed as a product for visitors, in a place where they have no commercial value at all — is the purpose the source names on the other side. That is not a verdict on anybody living. It is a verdict on the film's own reason for being there, which is the only place it can honestly land, and the last beat says so.

C021 stops the argument from collapsing into blame. Desire-to-act is the wish to take a thing up and expressly not the force that makes one adhere to it [C021-P:L69]; the Margaya says it resembles greed a little but has no adhering quality at all [C021-M:L27]. Effort is the part that does not turn back until the thing begun is finished [C021-M:L19], and the boat image makes it neutral: downstream where the mind already leans, uphill where it does not [C021-P:L53]. Three hundred years of that is standing in the pasture in dead coral, four metres high, running to the horizon, with a gap in it, holding nothing. And the six factors are called scattered precisely because they come and go and are found on both the wholesome and the unwholesome side [C021-P:L25] [C021-M:L3], which is the source's own reason why no mental state can be read off a wall or off an animal — the reason the film has no person in it and narrates nothing as anyone's greed.

One last piece of the record does doctrinal work rather than decorative work. Nobody agrees how many horses there are. The wildlife department's own park publication prints about four hundred to five hundred in a ranger's account and about a thousand in its species description, on facing pages; the IUCN assessment's figure of about a thousand appears in its tourism chapter and not in its biodiversity survey, which gives no count at all; a conservation programme reports about four hundred and fifty for 2014 and proposes an equine census that would establish a figure for the first time. The source's account of decision is exact about this: it settles firmly on an object without distinguishing true from false, and is frequently firm and wrong [C021-P:L45], while the other source calls it hard to notice happening at all [C021-M:L15]. The film therefore puts no number on screen as a count, and says instead that nobody agrees — which is both what is true and what the doctrine predicts.
what_is_certain: The island is low, porous coralline, semi-arid, dominated by palmyra palms, thorny shrubs and grasses, with a coastline of coral reef, dead coral outcrop and rubble beach, and it lies about 10 km off the mainland in the Palk Strait, reached by boat from the Kurikadduwan jetty on Punkudutivu; the crossing is about 14 km and takes roughly forty-five minutes to an hour.

Annual rainfall is about 750 mm, the rainy season runs roughly October to February, and the island has a pronounced drought from about June to September. Two inland lakes, Vedduk Kulam and Periya Kulam, are recorded. The Department of Wildlife Conservation supplies water by bowser to tanks in the park during the dry period, and its own publication records that animals die during that period nonetheless.

The Portuguese held Jaffna from 1597 to 1658 and their writing names the island first Ilha das Vacas, the island of cows, and then Ilha das Cavallos, the island of horses. They are reported to have built a fort on the coast, ploughed the land to prepare artificial pasture for horses and cattle, and introduced the horses, and to have taught the islanders to use a lasso.
The Dutch took Jaffna in 1658 and Rijckloff van Goens named the eight principal islands after Dutch cities, this one after Delft in Holland.

Philippus Baldaeus, minister of the Dutch Reformed Church, accompanied the Dutch troops that took Jaffna and published his description of Malabar, Coromandel and Ceylon in 1672. As quoted in the 2013 IUCN assessment he describes 'these horses that were brought into the Delft, which, multiplying in time, produced a certain kind of horses that are very small but hardy and fit to travel on stony and rocky ground ... they live in the wilderness and are taken by catching them in snares or ropes'. The sentence does not name who brought them, and it already describes the animals as living wild and being taken by snare.

In 1811 Lieutenant Edward Nolan, an Irishman of the 4th Ceylon Regiment serving in the Engineers Division under the Rt. Hon. John Wilson, Lieutenant-Governor and Commander-in-Chief in and over the British settlements in Ceylon, was given the task of growing flax (Linum usitatissimum) on the island to supply the government with canvas. In the following year he was additionally given the task of breeding the horses introduced by Portuguese and Dutch settlers, and he introduced several new breeding stocks.

As British cavalry demand grew, horses were shipped from the island to the small island of Iranaitivu for pasturage because the island could not produce enough fodder, and the island came to be known as 'the Horse Plains'.

Nolan built three sets of stone stables — recorded as one in the western part for untamed horses, one in the central part for trained horses and one in the eastern part used for training — and a series of wells cut with gradually sloping ramps down to the water so that animals could walk down to drink. The IUCN assessment states that those wells remain the island's main source of fresh water.

Nolan kept about sixty pigeons on the island, housed in a limestone dovecote that still stands near the divisional secretariat premises, and used them to communicate with contacts on the peninsula. In 1819 a petition signed by forty-five islanders was sent to the British Resident at Jaffna over his conduct towards the women of the island; the charges were dismissed, and he ruled the island until he retired from the service and returned to Ireland in 1824.

The surviving stable at Sarappiddy is about 150 m long and 10 m wide, built on two rows of thirty-six square pillars about 3 feet thick, with a gable wall about 6 m high still standing and many columns broken. It was maintained by successive administrators until 1870 and then abandoned, and it was declared a protected archaeological monument by gazette notification No. 1868 of 20 June 2014.

Philip K. Crowe, United States ambassador, toured the island in 1954 and used the British records to identify its monuments. He attributes the island's characteristic field walls to Nolan as Irish-style fences, built of coral where in Ireland they would be built of rock, and records that the islanders have continued the practice. He also observed that the stallions appeared to be better types than the mares and that 'no new blood has been introduced since the British period by Lt. Nolan in 1824'.

The 2013 IUCN assessment states explicitly that the stables and wells built by Nolan are at present attributed to the Dutch by the island's inhabitants and by recently published tourist guides, citing Liyanage (2011) and Ranatunga (2010).

Two stone towers on the island date from the British period and were used as navigational marks for daytime shipping and as a trigonometric point. The one known as the Queen's Tower survives, reported at about 55 feet in five diminishing stages of limestone block; only the base of the King's Tower remains.
A coral-and-limestone fort stands on the coast, two storeys, the ground floor reported as used for gunpowder and for holding prisoners.

The horses are a feral population of Equus caballus, locally called the Delft pony, recorded in the island's grassland habitats. The 2013 IUCN assessment states that except for a few families who keep captive animals there is no commercial value for the wild horses of the island at present, that they are allowed to roam freely at the far end of the island, and that the viewing of them could be developed into an attractive product for tourists.

The same assessment records that cattle released to graze because of a lack of fodder compete with the horses for pasture, that high cattle and pony mortality occurs at the height of the dry season for want of food and water, and that some people capture and mark the ponies' calves using improper branding methods, which can cause infections and is a major cause of death among calves.
In the 2011 dry season the Divisional Secretary, Alavipillai Siri, reported that about five per cent of the wild horse and cattle populations died for lack of water, and the navy built water troughs.

1,846.2 hectares of the island were declared Delft National Park under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance by special gazette notification dated 22 June 2015, managed by the Department of Wildlife Conservation. The southern part of the island had been recommended as a protected area for the horses in the 2013 IUCN assessment and again in an integrated strategic environmental assessment for the northern province of October 2014.

Recorded biodiversity in the park, per the Department of Wildlife Conservation: 209 species of flowering plants, 29 species of shrubs, 67 non-flowering species and about 70 herbs; 11 mammal species, 1 amphibian, 8 reptiles, 101 birds, 15 butterflies and 10 dragonflies. A flying fox colony was recorded at the baobab tree.

The island carries one large hollow baobab, Adansonia digitata, an African species held to have been introduced to South and South-East Asia by Arab sailors. Its trunk is hollow and can be entered and stood in by several people.

A peer-reviewed phenotypic study of the island's ponies exists: Jayathilake, Thananjayan, Alexander, de Silva and Pushpakumara, 'Phenotypic characterization of captive ponies in Delft island, Sri Lanka', Sri Lanka Veterinary Journal 67(1-2), 2020, 37-43. It measured ten captive animals (nine male, one female), all brown with no markings, taken from the feral population when young, average weight 85.66 kg with a standard deviation of 17.41 kg. It assigns no breed and gives no island population figure.
what_is_disputed: How many horses there are. No census was found. The Department of Wildlife Conservation's own park publication gives 'about 400 to 500 medium sized horses' in a ranger's account and 'about 1000 of them' in its species description, in the same document. The 2013 IUCN assessment says 'the wild horse is estimated to be around 1,000 at present' — a figure that appears in its tourism chapter, not in its biodiversity survey, which records the feral population with no count at all and states no method. A conservation programme reports the estimated population at about 450 for 2014 and proposes an equine census, which implies that none has been carried out. The figure of 'roughly five hundred' that circulates in travel writing and in this project's own earlier note therefore has no traceable basis; it is one of at least three numbers in play, the range in the sources runs from about 400 to about 1,000, and the figures are recorded here separately and never averaged.

Who brought the horses. The dominant account in the modern literature is the Portuguese, in the sixteenth century. The attribution is sourced but the chain is thin and late: no Portuguese document naming the importation was found; the Portuguese-period evidence is the pair of toponyms (island of cows, island of horses) and the report that they prepared pasture and taught the lasso; Baldaeus in 1672 says only that the horses 'were brought into the Delft'; and the explicit attribution in circulation rests on Crowe's 1954 reading of the records and on the heritage and assessment literature that followed him. Two further specifics are unsupported by anything found here: that the horses came 'from Arabia', which the wildlife department's park publication asserts and no other source consulted supports, and 'the sixteenth century', since the Portuguese held Jaffna only from 1597. The same wildlife department publication contradicts itself outright, its ranger interview stating that the horses 'were brought in to haul goods during Dutch era'. Popular accounts variously attribute them to the Portuguese, the Dutch, the British, or all three, and two Wikimedia photographers' own captions of the same herd disagree.

What the Dutch actually ran, and from when. That the island was used in the Dutch period to breed and distribute imported horses is stated by the IUCN assessment, and that they were bred by the Dutch and sold to ships passing the island is stated by the wildlife department. But Baldaeus in 1672, within about fourteen years of the Dutch arrival, describes the animals as living in the wilderness and being taken with snares or ropes, which is harvesting a feral herd rather than running a stud. No source consulted gives a start date for Dutch breeding; the date 'about 1660' carried in this project's earlier note is a rounding of the start of the Dutch period (Jaffna fell in 1658) and is not sourced. Whether there was ever a Dutch stud farm in the sense the phrase implies is not established; the stables that are shown to visitors as Dutch are Nolan's.

The coral walls. This project's earlier note had them built in the Dutch period, probably to pen the horses. Neither half survived research. The best-sourced account, Crowe's from the British records, makes them Irish-style field fences laid out under Nolan in the 1810s or 1820s and continued by the islanders to the present day, so a large and unknown proportion of them are modern. Wikipedia dates them to British colonial times. Popular Sri Lankan heritage writing attributes them to the Portuguese, the Dutch and the British together, and gives a height of around four metres and mortarless construction. No source found describes them as horse pens; they are described as field walls, and the island's grazing is open.

The stables and the wells. The IUCN assessment attributes them to Nolan and says so against the prevailing local and guidebook attribution to the Dutch; Sri Lankan heritage pages still carry them under the Dutch name; a heritage page citing the Department of Archaeology dates Nolan's administration of the island to 1813-1819 and the stables to that span, while the assessment, following Crowe, has him tasked with flax in 1811, with horses in 1812, and ruling until 1824. The two accounts are not reconciled here.

The fort. Katiresu identified the surviving coastal building as a Dutch fort in 1905; Nelson rejected that identification in 1984; later books list it as Portuguese; the assessment takes Baldaeus's 1672 illustration to show a Portuguese structure. The film records that its identity is contested.

When Nolan's officer was Governor. The IUCN assessment gives John Wilson's title correctly as Lieutenant-Governor and Commander-in-Chief; a Sri Lankan heritage page calls him Governor, which he was not.

The baobab's dimensions and age. The wildlife department gives the trunk as about 12 m high and 15 m in circumference. Travel writing gives 'a 52-foot hollow trunk' without saying whether that is height or girth, and this project's earlier note had it as about 52 feet round; one site gives more than 7 m in circumference. The tree is variously said to be over 400 years old, planted by Arab traders in the seventh century, and planted in the sixteenth. The often-quoted circumference of 19.5 m belongs to a different tree, the one at Pallimunai on Mannar island, which is the largest and oldest in the country. The wildlife department's claim that Sri Lanka has only two baobabs is wrong: about forty survive, of which thirty-four have been identified and measured on Mannar.

The island's size and shape. The IUCN assessment and the wildlife department give about 50 square kilometres, oval, maximum length 8 km and maximum width 6 km. Wikipedia gives 62 square kilometres, length 11 km and width 6 km. The human population is given as approximately 4,800 as of 2013, about 4,500, and approximately 5,000, against 12,000 in 1960, 6,200 in 1981 and 4,124 in 2007.

Present ownership of the horses, which is genuinely unresolved rather than merely unrecorded. The state protects 1,846.2 hectares of their range as a national park and waters them in the drought. The IUCN assessment says they have no commercial value and are allowed to roam. Press reporting says the animals generally carry brands, that many of them therefore still have owners, and that islanders continue to take them with snares from horseback; the same assessment records unauthorised branding of calves as a welfare problem. A 2020 veterinary paper measured ten captive animals taken young from the feral herd. Whether a branded feral horse inside a national park is legally anybody's property under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance was not established in this research, and nothing found addresses it. The film's line is that they are kept by nobody in particular, which is what the sources support and is not the same as saying they are ownerless.
The frequently repeated claim that this is the only place in the world with wild ponies, which appears on Wikipedia's page for the park. It is not true, and the film does not carry it.

The claim that the ponies' genetics preserve extinct sixteenth-century Iberian breeds, which circulates on travel and aggregator sites. No genetic study of this population was found. The only peer-reviewed work located is a phenotypic description of ten captive animals, which assigns no breed.

what_to_film: The island from very high, on the crossing and over the interior, for the grid of white walls across pale ground with the sea on two or three sides of the frame. This is the establishing statement and it needs the walls to read as a system rather than as a fence.

The surviving stable at Sarappiddy at ground level in flat white noon light: the full hundred and fifty metres of roofless colonnade down its own axis, the two rows of pillars, the standing gable wall, the broken columns, and dry grass through the floor. This is the payoff frame and everything else is built around getting it. No chalking, wetting, sweeping or lighting of stone.
One wall at eye level for its full run to the horizon, with the mortarless coral blocks close enough to read, and then a gap in it with open ground on both sides.

A ramped well from above and from the ramp itself, showing the slope cut for animals to walk down to water; and a water trough and tank in the pasture. Wildlife department water deliveries are filmed as objects and infrastructure, never as a scene with staff performing it.

The horses on a long lens from the greatest workable distance: the herd as small shapes in an empty bleached plain with nothing else vertical, standing, grazing and moving off at their own speed. Several separate long holds rather than one pursued sequence. If the animals react to the camera's presence in any way, the position is abandoned rather than adjusted.

The hollow baobab from outside only, whole, with the doorway-sized opening visible and its scale readable against the flat ground; and the flying fox colony recorded at the tree, if it is there, from a distance.
The limestone dovecote with its rows of empty holes, close and square-on.
The coastal fort and the surviving stepped tower, filmed as fabric and shape, without entering the contested question of who built the fort.
The bleached pasture with no animals in it at all, held long, with wind in the grass and the sea behind on two sides. This is the last shot and the film ends on a cut, not a move.
suggested_location.access: By boat from the Kurikadduwan jetty on Punkudutivu, about 46 km from Jaffna city centre; the crossing is roughly 14 km and takes about forty-five minutes to an hour. A free service is provided for passengers by the Road Development Authority using large navy-operated boats, with several sailings from around half past eight in the morning, and privately operated boats and hired boats also run. A bus service, scooter taxis, tractors and bicycles are available on the island. Three separate permissions bear on this film and none of them is assumable: the southern pastures are Delft National Park under the Department of Wildlife Conservation, entered under its rules; the surviving stable is a protected archaeological monument under the Department of Archaeology; and drone flight over a national park, over animals, and over a northern island served by naval vessels should be treated as prohibited until specifically and separately cleared in writing. Work is in Tamil and consent is asked in Tamil by somebody who speaks it. A day trip is governed by the sailings at both ends, which means the middle of the day — the film's own light — is the only reliable working window unless accommodation on the island is arranged.
suggested_location.best_time: The late dry season, roughly June to September, when the pasture is bleached, the walls are whitest and the light is flat and hard through the middle of the day; the rains fall roughly October to February and green the ground. The dry months are also when the animals are under the most water stress, so the same season that gives the film its look requires the greatest distance and the shortest time near them; if that trade cannot be kept, the animals are filmed in the greener season and the walls and the stable in the dry one, on two trips. Middle of the day is deliberate and is the group's only film built on noon light.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search on 26 September 2026 and none of it has been checked on the ground, with any authority, or against a printed edition. The two documents that carry most of the weight were read directly rather than through search summaries: the Department of Wildlife Conservation's own park publication (env.gov.lk, ten pages, comprising a ranger's account by G. U. Saranga, a park description, and species lists, edited by the Ministry of Wildlife and Forest Resources Conservation), and the 2013 IUCN and Government of Sri Lanka assessment (Goonatilake, Ekanayake, Kumara, Liyanapathirana, Weerakoon and Wadugodapitiya, 'Sustainable Development of Delft Island: An ecological, socio-economic and archaeological assessment', Occasional Papers of IUCN Sri Lanka No. 14, January 2013, viii + 86 pp.), which was downloaded and read at the relevant pages. Both are Sri Lankan government or government-partnered publications and both are internally inconsistent about the horses, which is recorded in what_is_disputed rather than resolved. The coordinates given are the IUCN assessment's GPS point for the horse stable, which is the film's fixed anchor; the same table gives the baobab at 9.512480 N, 79.715391 E and the coral depression called Adam's foot at 9.51796 N, 79.65824 E, and the island's own centre is about 9.5167 N, 79.6833 E. Baldaeus is quoted as the IUCN assessment quotes him in English, not from any edition of the 1672 text, and the wording of the quotation could not be checked; his presence on the island in 1672 is asserted by the assessment, while the standard account has him in Jaffna from 1658 and his book published in 1672 after his return, so the assessment's 'visited Delft Island' in 1672 may be a compression and is not relied on for anything beyond the quoted observation. Crowe (1954) is used entirely at second hand through the IUCN assessment, which cites him for the Irish-style fences, the stables and wells, Nolan's administration and the remark about stallions and mares; his book was not read. The stable's measurements, its abandonment in 1870 and the 2014 archaeological gazette come from a Sri Lankan heritage site citing the Department of Archaeology's 'The archaeological heritage of Jaffna peninsula' (Dias, Koralage and Asanga, 2016), Wijebandara (2014) and the Gazette No. 1868 of 20 June 2014; neither the gazette nor the departmental volume was seen. The national park's area and its gazette date of 22 June 2015 are consistent between the wildlife department's publication and Wikipedia's park article. The veterinary paper on captive ponies was read as an abstract only. Three things in the brief this record was written against turned out to be wrong and are corrected here rather than carried: the coral walls are not established as Dutch and are not described by any source as horse pens, the best-sourced account making them Irish-style field fences laid out under a British officer and still being built by islanders today; there is no basis for 'roughly five hundred' horses, and the range across sources runs from about 400 to about 1,000 with the wildlife department printing two of those numbers in one document; and the baobab's girth is given as 15 m by the wildlife department, so the '52 feet round' figure is unsourced and may be a garbling of a height. No census of the horses was found and a conservation programme's proposal for an equine census implies none exists. Whether a branded feral horse inside a national park is legally anybody's property was not established. No official, resident, wildlife officer, archaeological officer or community representative has been approached, no drone clearance has been sought or assessed, the ferry sailings and their reliability were not verified with any operator, and the Wikimedia images were each confirmed to exist through the Commons query API on 26 September 2026 but are of the island and its features rather than of any planned frame.

unknowns: No census of the horses exists as far as this research can establish, and the published figures range from about 400 to about 1,000. The film's own line is that nobody agrees; if a census is completed before filming, the record needs revising.

Whether a branded feral horse inside a national park is anybody's legal property under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance. Nothing found addresses it, and the question bears directly on how the film may describe the animals.

Whether filming permission in the national park would be given, on what conditions, and whether those conditions would allow the long-lens distance the film requires rather than a guided approach to the animals.

Whether drone flight is permitted over the island at all, given a national park, a naval-operated crossing and a northern province; the establishing shot of the wall grid depends on it and may simply be refused.
Whether permission to film the protected stable is separate from the park permission, and who grants it.
How much of the wall network is colonial and how much was built by islanders in the last century, which the film should not misstate and which no source consulted quantifies.
Whether accommodation on the island can be arranged, without which the sailings decide the working day.
No official, resident, wildlife officer or archaeological officer has been approached. Everything here is a research direction.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Claude's suggestion and awaits Chathura's verdict; its supporting detail is desk research and is unverified. The historical thread rests on two government or government-partnered publications that contradict each other about this film's own subject, and those contradictions are recorded rather than resolved. No scene or shot is decided here.
